a.picturePrompt: In which story does a visitor bring news to a family?

bonuses.prompt: Who brought the news about the baby?
options: An angel
A shepherd
A king
bonuses.explanation: An angel came to speak to the baby's mother.

bonuses.prompt: What did the mother do after the visit?
options: Built a house
Told the father
Drew water
bonuses.explanation: She went and told Manoah what she had heard.

lessons.prompt: What did his mother name him?
options: Noah
Samson
Moses
Joshua
lessons.explanation: After her son was born, his mother named him Samson.

lessons.prompt: Why did the father want the visitor to come back?
options: To plant a tree
To find a sheep
To learn how to care for the child
To fix a door
lessons.explanation: Manoah wanted help getting ready for the baby.

b.picturePrompt: The path leads to a field. What news did Samson’s mother receive there?

bonuses.prompt: What was Samson's father's name?
options: Manoah
Noah
Moses
bonuses.explanation: Samson's father was Manoah. He asked for guidance on raising the child.

bonuses.prompt: When the angel returned, who went to fetch Manoah?
options: His son
His wife
A neighbor
bonuses.explanation: She saw the visitor in the field and hurried to tell her husband.

lessons.prompt: What does Manoah want to learn before the baby is born?
options: How to care for the child
Where Samson will live as an adult
Which city will choose a new king
When the family should travel to Timnah
lessons.explanation: He asks for the messenger to come back and teach them what to do for the boy.

lessons.prompt: The messenger says the child will begin to help Israel. What is his family being prepared for?
options: Their son must finish his task on the day he is born
His father will do everything in his place
His family must move away before his birth
Their son will grow up with a task beyond his own home
lessons.explanation: The news is about both a new baby and the help he will one day give his people.

c.picturePrompt: Which announcement in Judges is suggested by a meeting in a field?

bonuses.prompt: Which detail is not given in Judges 13?
options: The name of Samson's mother
Manoah's name
The child's name
bonuses.explanation: Samson's mother plays a central role, but the chapter does not name her.

bonuses.prompt: Which instruction does the angel personally give the mother during the first encounter?
options: Return with Manoah
Refrain from wine
Offer a young goat
bonuses.explanation: Judges 13:4 addresses her diet. Manoah's meeting and his offering come later.

lessons.prompt: The messenger links the child's uncut hair with which aspect of his calling?
options: A vow his mother is to make at birth
A dedication already in force before birth
A vow he will take on becoming a judge
A dedication conditional on defeating the Philistines
lessons.explanation: The announcement ties the ban on cutting his hair to a calling that begins in the womb.

lessons.prompt: Manoah reads the encounter as a sign they will die. Which two things does his wife use to challenge him?
options: The angel hid his name and refused their invitation to eat
Manoah prayed for a second visit and the angel returned
Their offering was accepted and they received news of what was to come
The angel rose in the flame and the couple fell to the ground
lessons.explanation: Each detail belongs to the encounter. In verse 23 she argues specifically from what God accepted, showed and announced.

teen.picturePrompt: Which event does the light in the field point to, before the hero of the story is even born?

bonuses.prompt: Who hears the news about Samson directly from the visitor on his first visit?
options: His mother
His father
Both parents together
bonuses.explanation: Manoah hears about the first visit from his wife.

bonuses.prompt: The messenger describes a child set apart for God. What sign of that calling will others be able to see?
options: He will carry a staff
His hair will grow uncut
He will wear a crown
bonuses.explanation: The instruction about his hair gives his dedication a visible sign.

lessons.prompt: Manoah offers the visitor a meal. The visitor directs him to make an offering to God. What distinction is he making?
options: The messenger brings the news, but the offering belongs to God
The visitors in the two meetings are different people
Only Manoah’s wife may give thanks for the promise
The meal must wait until after Samson is born
lessons.explanation: The visitor redirects Manoah’s wish to honor his guest toward the one who sent him.

lessons.prompt: The messenger says Samson will begin to deliver Israel. What does the word “begin” leave open?
options: Whether the Philistines rule Israel at the time of his birth
Whether the child in the promise is a son or a daughter
Whether Israel is the people he will help
When Israel’s deliverance will be complete
lessons.explanation: The promise gives Samson a part in setting Israel free. It does not say when the whole struggle will end.

a.picturePrompt: Which story do the large pawprints on the path suggest?

bonuses.prompt: Which animal roared at Samson on the road?
options: A bear
A goat
A lion
bonuses.explanation: A young lion came roaring toward him.

bonuses.prompt: What was Samson holding when he overcame the lion?
options: Nothing
A sword
A staff
bonuses.explanation: Samson overcame the lion with his bare hands. The account says he had nothing in his hand.

lessons.prompt: Who traveled toward Timnah with Samson?
options: His parents
Two shepherds
A king and queen
His brothers
lessons.explanation: Samson set out with his father and mother.

lessons.prompt: Why didn't his parents hear about the lion from Samson?
options: They asked for honey
He forgot the way
He kept it to himself
They had stayed at home
lessons.explanation: The story says that he did not tell his parents what had happened.

b.picturePrompt: Which encounter near a vineyard do these large pawprints suggest?

bonuses.prompt: What is true of the moment Samson meets the lion?
options: He is returning from Timnah after collecting honey
He has already told his guests about the honey
He is on the way to Timnah, before finding honey
bonuses.explanation: He meets the lion on his first journey. Finding honey belongs to another visit.

bonuses.prompt: Which event happened on a later visit?
options: Finding the honey
Setting out for Timnah
Hearing the lion roar
bonuses.explanation: The bees and honey appear when Samson returns after some time.

lessons.prompt: What detail shows that Samson did not rely on equipment?
options: He was near a vineyard
His hands were empty
He was walking to Timnah
His parents were on the road
lessons.explanation: The narrator points out that Samson held nothing in his hand.

lessons.prompt: Why could Samson’s parents make the journey with him and still miss part of his story?
options: They had only heard a story about the spring
They thought he had stayed at home
They had set out to find his wedding guests
He kept the encounter with the lion to himself
lessons.explanation: They were traveling to the same place, but Samson did not tell them everything that happened to him.

c.picturePrompt: Which episode on the road to Timnah is pictured here?

bonuses.prompt: Which phrase locates Samson's first encounter with the lion?
options: The rock of Etam
The valley of Sorek
The vineyards of Timnah
bonuses.explanation: Judges 14:5 places the encounter near the vineyards on the journey to Timnah.

bonuses.prompt: What does the first visit establish that a reader must remember on the return visit?
options: The encounter with the lion and Samson’s silence about it
The discovery of honey and its sharing with his parents
The terms of the wager and the riddle’s wording
bonuses.explanation: The later visit gains its meaning from the earlier encounter and the knowledge gap left by his silence.

lessons.prompt: What does the narrator explicitly place immediately before Samson overpowers the lion?
options: Samson recalls the vow made before his birth
The spirit of the Lord comes upon him
Samson calls on God for strength
His parents hear the lion's roar
lessons.explanation: Judges 14:6 introduces the act with the coming of the spirit. No speech or prayer by Samson intervenes.

lessons.prompt: What does Samson keep from his parents across his two visits to the same place?
options: First the trip to Timnah, then the encounter with the lion
First the source of the honey, then the terms of the wager
First the encounter with the lion, then the source of the honey
First the approaching wedding, then the honey he gathered
lessons.explanation: Judges 14:6 and 14:9 each mark a silence. His parents receive the honey, but the reader alone shares both discoveries with him.

teen.picturePrompt: Which encounter on the road to Timnah do the tracks among the vines suggest?

bonuses.prompt: What changes between the tracks and the roar in the account?
options: A mark on the ground already reveals who will get honey
The roar tells the parents what has already happened
A sign of an animal nearby becomes a direct encounter with a young lion
bonuses.explanation: Tracks suggest an animal’s presence. The roar takes place in the encounter itself.

bonuses.prompt: The narrator mentions both the spirit of the Lord and Samson’s empty hands. What does each detail add?
options: One explains his strength and the other shows he had no weapon
One names the place and the other gives the time
One describes the lion and the other describes the vineyard
bonuses.explanation: The first detail links his strength to God. The second shows how unexpected the outcome was.

lessons.prompt: Which claim about Samson’s parents goes beyond what these verses tell us?
options: They were on the journey to Timnah
They knew about the lion from the start
Samson did not tell them about his encounter
Their son faced a lion near the vineyards
lessons.explanation: Their presence on the journey does not tell us they witnessed the encounter.

lessons.prompt: Suppose the wedding guests already knew what had happened near the vineyard. How would that change the later contest?
options: There would be no bees on the return journey
His parents would no longer travel to Timnah
The wedding would take place in the vineyard
The guests would have a clue to the riddle’s strong creature
lessons.explanation: Keeping the encounter private later gives Samson an advantage when he poses his riddle.

a.picturePrompt: In which story does Samson find something sweet?

bonuses.prompt: What sweet food did Samson find when he returned to the place where he had met the lion?
options: Grapes
Honey
Dates
bonuses.explanation: On his later visit, Samson found bees and honey. The honey became part of his riddle.

bonuses.prompt: Where did Samson tell the guests his riddle?
options: Beside a spring
At the city gate
At a feast
bonuses.explanation: Samson told the riddle at his wedding feast in Timnah.

lessons.prompt: Which happened first?
options: Samson found honey there
The guests heard a riddle
Samson met the lion
The guests gave their answer
lessons.explanation: The lion came first. The honey and the riddle came later.

lessons.prompt: Why did Samson use the word sweet in his riddle?
options: He had tasted honey
He had picked figs
He had baked a cake
He had eaten dates
lessons.explanation: The sweet thing Samson knew about was the honey he had found.

b.picturePrompt: Which challenge did Samson make up after finding honey on the road?

bonuses.prompt: What did Samson see beside the honey when he returned to the lion?
options: A flock of birds
A swarm of bees
A herd of goats
bonuses.explanation: The bees and their honey were in the remains of the lion.

bonuses.prompt: What did Samson do with some of his find before the feast?
options: Hid it at the city gate
Took it to the guests as a prize
Gave it to his parents
bonuses.explanation: His parents ate it without learning where it came from.

lessons.prompt: How did the guests learn the answer?
options: It was written on the table
The lion led them to it
Manoah read it aloud
Samson's wife told them after they pressured her
lessons.explanation: The guests pressured Samson's wife to get the answer and pass it on.

lessons.prompt: What makes the words strong and sweet fit the same riddle?
options: The lion had eaten at the feast
Two discoveries were made in the same place
The honey gave Samson strength
The guests brought the lion and the honey
lessons.explanation: Samson links the strength of the lion to the sweetness of the honey he later found there.

c.picturePrompt: Which event in Judges 14 links the vineyard to the feast?

bonuses.prompt: How does the role of the secret change from vineyard to feast?
options: A shared family experience becomes a test already familiar to the guests
An untold experience becomes the basis of a wager only its keeper can solve from experience
The guests’ knowledge becomes a secret Samson wants to buy from them
bonuses.explanation: Readers learn where the answer came from, but the guests have no access to the private event.

bonuses.prompt: What did Samson's parents know after they ate the honey?
options: They knew where he found it, but not when he returned there
They knew about the lion, but not about the bees
They knew who gave it to them, but not where he found it
bonuses.explanation: Samson hands them the honey yet keeps its source from them, having also withheld his earlier encounter.

lessons.prompt: Which pair correctly follows the two halves of the riddle in their stated order?
options: An eater yields food; something strong yields sweetness
Something strong yields food; an eater yields sweetness
Food yields an eater; sweetness yields something strong
Sweetness yields strength; an eater yields food
lessons.explanation: The two halves in Judges 14:14 move in parallel from the lion's qualities to the honey found in it.

lessons.prompt: Whose access to knowledge explains how the guests can answer a riddle drawn from Samson's private experience?
options: They pressure his wife; she learns about the honey from his parents
His parents recognize the honey and tell his wife what it means
They pressure his wife; she learns the answer from him and tells them
His wife witnesses his discovery and tells the guests what she saw
lessons.explanation: The guests' pressure reaches Samson through his wife; the answer then travels back through her.

teen.picturePrompt: Which challenge at a feast do the honey and the traces of a lion bring to mind?

bonuses.prompt: Which experience gave Samson the idea for the sweet food in his challenge?
options: Tasting wine at his wedding
Finding honey where he had encountered the lion
Receiving fruit from his guests
bonuses.explanation: The answer draws on a discovery Samson made before the feast.

bonuses.prompt: Who can link strength and sweetness before the riddle is solved, and why?
options: Samson’s parents, because tasting honey always reveals where it came from
The guests, because hearing a riddle reveals its secret
The reader and Samson, because both know about the two visits
bonuses.explanation: The narrator has given us the connection Samson experienced. Others have not been told the honey’s source.

lessons.prompt: How does the guests’ pressure on Samson’s wife change the contest?
options: The guests decide to give up the prize
Everyone is allowed to change the riddle
The guests begin looking for bees in the vineyards
Getting access to his secret matters more than solving the wordplay
lessons.explanation: Instead of explaining the words on their own, the guests seek someone who can learn the answer from him.

lessons.prompt: Why can the reader follow both sides of the argument at the feast?
options: Samson explains his discovery to everyone before they answer
We have seen both Samson’s discovery and how the guests learned his secret
The guests find another lion and another swarm
His parents settle the argument by telling everyone what they saw
lessons.explanation: The narrator takes the reader from the road to the feast and shows what each side knows.

a.picturePrompt: The ropes are ready beside the rock. In which story can they no longer hold Samson by the end?

bonuses.prompt: Why did the men bring ropes when they came for Samson?
options: To keep his hands tied
To lift him up with them
For him to carry to the people at Lehi
bonuses.explanation: The men of Judah meant to lead him away with his hands tied.

bonuses.prompt: What had already happened when the ropes broke?
options: The men of Judah were still looking for him
The men of Judah had tied Samson
Samson had just reached his hiding place
bonuses.explanation: They found him and tied him first. The ropes broke when he reached Lehi.

lessons.prompt: What happened to the ropes at Lehi?
options: They became a bridge
They broke away
They grew leaves
They became a gate
lessons.explanation: Samson received strength and broke free.

lessons.prompt: After the ropes broke, what could Samson do again?
options: Find honey in a tree
Hear the angel
Move his arms freely
See a spring appear
lessons.explanation: With the ropes gone, his arms were free.

bonuses.prompt: Why did new ropes suit the men of Judah’s plan?
options: They expected fresh rope to hold Samson on the journey
They wanted the ropes to guide Samson to his hiding place
They wanted Samson to take the ropes back to Lehi
bonuses.explanation: They intended to hand him over bound, so they chose rope that looked strong.

bonuses.prompt: Which route fits the order of events?
options: From Lehi to Etam, where the ropes broke
From the hiding place at Etam to Lehi, where the ropes broke
From Etam to Lehi after the ropes had already broken in hiding
bonuses.explanation: He was bound at Etam, arrived bound at Lehi and broke free there.

lessons.prompt: What did the men of Judah promise Samson?
options: To make him king
To build him a house
To solve his riddle
Not to kill him themselves
lessons.explanation: They promised not to kill him before binding him.

lessons.prompt: The Philistines ruled the land. Why were the people of Judah worried about Samson’s quarrel with them?
options: They thought the Philistines might punish their people too
They hoped Samson would solve another riddle
They thought their spring had dried up
They wanted him to stay at the rock forever
lessons.explanation: The Philistines had come into Judah looking for Samson. His quarrel had reached other people as well.

b.picturePrompt: New ropes lie beside the rock. Which episode starts with their use as bindings and ends when they tear?

c.picturePrompt: Which episode in Judges 15 connects the ropes by the rock to the men of Judah handing Samson over?

bonuses.prompt: What tension arises between Judah’s undertaking to Samson and its response to Philistine rule?
options: They promise not to kill him themselves yet surrender him to his opponents
They promise complete freedom yet imprison him at Etam
They swear to oppose the Philistines and refuse to lead him to Lehi
bonuses.explanation: The oath limits what their own hands will do. It offers no protection from those who receive him.

bonuses.prompt: What do the men of Judah promise when Samson agrees to go with them?
options: To bind him only after the Philistines take custody
To hand him over without killing him themselves
To hand him over only if his captors spare him
bonuses.explanation: Their oath in Judges 15:13 binds the men of Judah to their own conduct and leaves his captors free of that promise.

lessons.prompt: What does the simile of flax touched by fire describe at Lehi?
options: The way the ropes had been prepared before binding
The loss of the new ropes' hold on Samson
The means the men of Judah used to free him
A signal the Philistines gave when he arrived
lessons.explanation: The simile follows the descent of the spirit; the bound arms are suddenly free.

lessons.prompt: What do the words of Judah's men and Samson's reply each stress about the conflict?
options: They stress their oath; he stresses his calling before birth
They stress a personal injury; he stresses freeing Judah from foreign rule
They stress Philistine rule; he stresses repaying what was done to him
They stress the danger of binding him; he stresses his duty as judge
lessons.explanation: Their exchange in Judges 15:11 puts the community's political position beside Samson's account of personal retaliation.

teen.picturePrompt: Which episode between the rock of Etam and Lehi is hinted at by the pair of new ropes?

bonuses.prompt: Why do the men of Judah want to bind Samson although they did not start the dispute?
options: They live under Philistine rule and fear the consequences of his actions
They know his secret and want to test it
They are acting on a treaty Samson made with the people of Lehi
bonuses.explanation: Their reference to Philistine rule explains both the fear and the decision to hand him over.

bonuses.prompt: What condition does Samson put on going with the men of Judah?
options: They must bring his parents to Lehi
They must promise not to attack him themselves
They must first free everyone in Judah
bonuses.explanation: He distinguishes what his own people may do from what the Philistines might do.

lessons.prompt: Why does the narrator call the ropes new before describing their breaking?
options: It tells us how many people brought them
It identifies which town made the ropes
It dates the scene to the beginning of the year
It makes worn-out ropes an unlikely explanation
lessons.explanation: The ropes seem dependable, so their sudden failure comes as a surprise.

lessons.prompt: The Philistines shout when they see Samson bound. What changes the meaning of that moment for the reader?
options: Their shout of apparent victory comes just before the bonds give way
Their shouting convinces Judah to take Samson home
Samson thinks they are calling him to a feast
They celebrate only after they see the ropes on the ground
lessons.explanation: The order of events overturns the expectation raised by Samson’s arrival as a captive.

a.picturePrompt: There is water among the dry rocks. In which story does Samson get the help he needed?

bonuses.prompt: Which help would meet thirsty Samson’s need?
options: Showing him a resting spot after a walk
Showing him where to wash his clothes
Showing him where to find drinking water
bonuses.explanation: He called for help because he was thirsty, and the spring gave him water to drink.

bonuses.prompt: Which came first, calling for help or drinking?
options: Samson asked for help and then drank
Samson drank and then asked for water
Samson called after he had drunk his fill
bonuses.explanation: He called while he was thirsty. Water appeared and he drank.

lessons.prompt: What happened after he drank?
options: He became king
A storm began
He recovered
The city emptied
lessons.explanation: The account describes his strength and vitality returning.

lessons.prompt: Samson could break strong ropes. Why did he still ask for help here?
options: He was thirsty and needed a drink
He wanted to give a wedding feast
He needed to carry a gate
He wanted to catch bees
lessons.explanation: Even someone very strong needs water.

bonuses.prompt: Which detail explains why Samson did not need to return to town to drink?
options: Someone carried water from town to the site
He was sent to a spring on the far side of town
Water came out right where he was at Lehi
bonuses.explanation: In the account, water comes from a hollow at Lehi itself.

bonuses.prompt: How does what happened after Samson drank answer his request?
options: He feared dying of thirst, and the drink revived him
He asked to rest, and the drink sent him back into battle
He asked the way to town, and the water showed it
bonuses.explanation: The water met the very danger Samson had described in his call.

lessons.prompt: Which action is recalled in the name En-hakkore, the spring of the caller?
options: The lion roaring at Samson
Samson calling for help
The guests asking a riddle
The men of Judah making a promise
lessons.explanation: The word for caller echoes the call Samson made before the water appeared.

lessons.prompt: Samson had broken the ropes at Lehi. Why couldn’t he simply use that strength again when he was thirsty?
options: The ropes had been tied again
Someone had carried away his cup
He needed his father to show him how to drink
Strong arms could not give him drinking water
lessons.explanation: At first he needed to get free. This time he needed water, so he called for help.

b.picturePrompt: The hollow in the rock recalls what followed Samson’s exertion at Lehi. Which episode links a call for help there with a drink?

c.picturePrompt: Which episode at Lehi do the waters emerging after Samson calls for help suggest?

bonuses.prompt: Which feature of Lehi is named as the source of the water?
options: The rock of Etam
The height called Ramath-lehi
The hollow there
bonuses.explanation: Judges 15:19 locates the opening in the hollow at Lehi.

bonuses.prompt: What reversal marks the move from broken ropes to the hollow at Lehi?
options: The one who overcame his captors now needs help to survive
The one who drank at Lehi now asks to be bound
The one given water refuses to credit God for the victory
bonuses.explanation: The call in thirst makes his dependence explicit just after a display of strength.

lessons.prompt: Which reading fits the two parts of Samson's prayer when he is thirsty?
options: He fears enemy capture, then asks to avenge what was done to him
He promises a memorial name, then asks God to give him water
He credits God with deliverance, then fears falling into enemy hands
He recalls his vow, then promises to serve if his strength returns
lessons.explanation: Samson places what God has already granted beside the danger he now faces.

lessons.prompt: How do the two place-names Ramath-lehi and En-hakkore mark different moments in the episode?
options: The first follows the discarded jawbone; the second recalls Samson's call for help
The first recalls Samson's thirst; the second recalls the cry of the Philistines
The first follows his prayer; the second recalls the jawbone he lifted in battle
The first recalls the Philistines' cry; the second recalls the death he feared
lessons.explanation: In Judges 15:17 the naming follows Samson throwing away the jawbone. In verse 19 the spring's name preserves his call.

teen.picturePrompt: Which named place in Samson’s story is suggested by water welling from a hollow at Lehi?

bonuses.prompt: To whom does Samson give credit for his victory as he starts his prayer?
options: To the men of Judah
To his father
To God
bonuses.explanation: Before asking for help, Samson recalls who gave him the victory.

bonuses.prompt: Why does the name En-hakkore preserve more than the memory of water?
options: It links the spring to Samson’s act of calling
It records only the shape of the hollow in the rock
It shows that Samson forced the rock open with his arms
bonuses.explanation: The name joins the source of water to the memory of the person who called for help.

lessons.prompt: Why does Samson speak about falling into enemy hands immediately after a victory?
options: The earlier victory belonged to the Philistines
He fears that thirst could undo what he has just achieved
He has already been taken to Gaza
He plans to return to the men who bound him
lessons.explanation: His prayer puts his recent success beside a danger that strength alone cannot solve.

lessons.prompt: What part of the story does the name En-hakkore, the caller’s spring, preserve for later visitors?
options: A champion won the place in a contest of strength
The people who dug the hollow founded a city
A guard used the spring to call travelers together
Someone in danger called out and received help there
lessons.explanation: The name recalls an appeal for help even though the place is also associated with a victory.

a.picturePrompt: In town the door blocks the way. In which story does it end up on the hill with Samson?

bonuses.prompt: Why was there an opening in the wall that nobody could shut?
options: Samson opened the doors for a moment
Samson took the doors away
Samson slid the bar across a door
bonuses.explanation: The doors themselves were gone from the wall.

bonuses.prompt: The townspeople were waiting for morning. How did Samson leave ahead of them?
options: He stayed until morning
He came back to town in the morning
He left in the middle of the night
bonuses.explanation: They were still waiting for daybreak when Samson left.

lessons.prompt: Where did Samson take the gates after lifting them?
options: Up a hill
Into a well
Into a boat
Down to a spring
lessons.explanation: The story follows him carrying the gates uphill.

lessons.prompt: Why did the people waiting until morning miss Samson's departure?
options: He stayed until noon
He waited for them to leave
He left the following evening
He left while it was still dark
lessons.explanation: Samson got up in the middle of the night, ahead of their plan.

bonuses.prompt: Why did leaving at midnight upset the plan of the people of Gaza?
options: They planned to wait on the hill at night
They planned to wait near the gate until morning
They planned to carry the gate away at midnight themselves
bonuses.explanation: The townspeople intended to wait for daylight. Samson left during the night.

bonuses.prompt: Which parts explain why an opening remained in the wall instead of just a broken bar?
options: The bar and hinges, with the doors still in place
One post and the bar, with the other post still standing
The doors, both posts and the bar
bonuses.explanation: The account describes the whole assembly being torn out and carried away.

lessons.prompt: What spoiled the plan to wait for Samson at daybreak?
options: He was given the key in the morning
Men from Judah untied him
He left the city at midnight
The guards went looking for water
lessons.explanation: His departure came hours before the time chosen by those lying in wait.

lessons.prompt: At Lehi the ropes broke, and in Gaza the gate was carried away. How were the ropes and the gate alike?
options: Both were meant to keep Samson from leaving
Both belonged to Samson’s family
Both were taken up the same hill
Both marked the place where he found water
lessons.explanation: In each place other people expected Samson to stay where he was. In both places he got away.

b.picturePrompt: In this picture the bar keeps the door in place. In which story do bar and door end up somewhere else together?

c.picturePrompt: Which deed in Judges 16 transforms a gate meant to trap Samson into a load on his shoulders?

bonuses.prompt: What does the phrase locating the hill “facing Hebron” establish about the illustrated journey?
options: The destination has to be central Hebron and the distance is given explicitly
The destination is described in relation to Hebron, but no distance is specified
The journey begins in Hebron and ends at the gate of Gaza
bonuses.explanation: A relative location is not a measurement of the journey.

bonuses.prompt: Which part came away together with the doors and gateposts?
options: The city wall
The outer watchtower
The crossbar
bonuses.explanation: Judges 16:3 lists the bar along with the doors and their two posts.

lessons.prompt: Which contrast between the ambushers' plan and Samson's action is explicit?
options: They gather at midnight; he reaches the hill at dawn
They leave by dawn; he lifts the gate after sunrise
They lock the gate at midnight; he waits until morning
They plan for dawn; he rises at midnight
lessons.explanation: The narrative gives the time the men intend to act and the time Samson rises; it leaves the arrival time unstated.

lessons.prompt: When explaining how Samson gets free, how do the accounts at Lehi and Gaza differ?
options: At Gaza the spirit comes upon him; at Lehi his actions are narrated without that phrase
At Lehi the spirit comes upon him; at Gaza his actions are narrated without that phrase
In both he first prays, and the lifting or breaking follows his prayer
In both the narrator first invokes the dedication announced before his birth
lessons.explanation: Judges 15:14 explicitly names the spirit. Judges 16:3 moves from rising at midnight straight to taking hold of the gate.

teen.picturePrompt: Which event joins the entrance to one city with a hill facing Hebron?

bonuses.prompt: What piece of news sets the people of Gaza watching the gate?
options: Their gate is already gone
Samson is in their city
The people of Hebron are coming
bonuses.explanation: Word of Samson’s arrival reaches the people of Gaza before the gate is moved.

bonuses.prompt: How do Samson’s actions answer the plan at Gaza in both time and place?
options: He waits for dawn as they do and uses another gate
He leaves at night but leaves the exit under their control
He acts before dawn and takes away the gate where they waited
bonuses.explanation: Midnight precedes the intended attack, and uprooting the gate changes the very place of the ambush.

lessons.prompt: Why does the narrator tell us what the people at the gate expect to happen in the morning?
options: It explains why the city has no gate at night
It tells us that Samson has heard every word they said
Their expectation makes Samson’s earlier departure a surprise
It proves that someone in Gaza warned him
lessons.explanation: We learn the plan before we learn what Samson does. His action overturns the expectation the plan creates.

lessons.prompt: What can we say for certain about Samson’s knowledge when he leaves Gaza?
options: The story tells when he acted but leaves open how much he knew about the plan
The narrator says he overheard the people at the gate
A friend from Hebron brought him a warning
God told him exactly when the guards would leave
lessons.explanation: The people’s plans and Samson’s actions are described. No warning or account of his thoughts is given.

a.picturePrompt: This time the clue is long hair beside a loom. In which story does someone try to learn what gives Samson strength?

bonuses.prompt: What did Delilah learn by talking that looking at his hair could not tell her?
options: Why the hair mattered to Samson
What color his hair was
How long his hair looked
bonuses.explanation: She could see its color and length. Samson had to tell her the secret.

bonuses.prompt: What had to happen before Delilah called the man over?
options: Samson woke and saw his hair
Samson told her his secret and fell asleep
The man had already finished cutting it
bonuses.explanation: Samson told her about his hair, then fell asleep. That was when she called.

lessons.prompt: First Samson kept his secret. What did he do after Delilah kept asking?
options: Went to see his parents
Lifted the city gate
Carried her to a spring
Told her his secret
lessons.explanation: At last he told Delilah about his hair.

lessons.prompt: Why did Delilah call someone over while Samson slept?
options: To have a rope untied
To have his long hair cut
To have a door opened
To have some water brought
lessons.explanation: After learning about his hair, Delilah arranged for it to be cut.

bonuses.prompt: Why did the leaders offer Delilah silver instead of immediately trying to bind Samson again?
options: Ropes had failed, and they wanted information they lacked
They already knew his secret and wanted to check his hair color
They wanted Delilah to pay the men who brought ropes
bonuses.explanation: The leaders wanted to discover the source of his great strength so they could overcome him.

bonuses.prompt: Which sequence explains how a private conversation led to cutting the hair?
options: The hair was cut first, and only then did Delilah ask for the secret
Samson told Delilah, she called others, then the hair was cut
The man told Samson the secret, and Samson called Delilah
bonuses.explanation: The information went from Samson to Delilah before the haircut could take place.

lessons.prompt: What does Samson's uncut hair represent?
options: A royal crown
His dedication to God as a Nazirite from birth
A way to control the weather
A rule everyone in Gaza followed
lessons.explanation: Samson connects his uncut hair to being a Nazirite, dedicated to God from birth.

lessons.prompt: What does Delilah's behavior have in common with the wedding guests' behavior?
options: They hear the answer from his parents
They all find honey on the way
They use pressure to discover a secret
They all tell Samson their own secret first
lessons.explanation: At the wedding the guests pressure Samson's wife. Here Delilah keeps pressing Samson himself.

b.picturePrompt: The hair and loom point to an attempt that has yet to reveal the secret. In which story will another conversation change Samson’s fate?

c.picturePrompt: Which episode sets the failed attempt at weaving hair against the later disclosure of a Nazirite secret?

bonuses.prompt: How does the rulers’ offer shape our reading of an apparently intimate exchange?
options: Each ruler promises silver, framing the search for the secret as a collective concern
Only one ruler makes a pledge, leaving the others uninterested
The payment is offered to Samson, making this a direct negotiation with him
bonuses.explanation: The pledge by each ruler brings political stakes into a conversation between two people.

bonuses.prompt: How does weaving the locks prepare for the final disclosure without repeating it?
options: The weaving already reveals his Nazirite status and he later repeats the same words
Hair enters a misleading answer before Samson links it to his dedication from birth
The weaving comes after the cutting and explains it retrospectively
bonuses.explanation: The story brings Delilah closer to his hair before Samson discloses its significance.

lessons.prompt: What information does the narrator give the reader when Samson wakes in Judges 16:20?
options: His hair has begun to grow, and Delilah is unaware of it
His strength has returned, and his captors are unaware of it
The Lord has left him, and Samson is unaware of it
The Philistines have left, and Samson is unaware of it
lessons.explanation: Samson expects to get free as before while the narrator gives readers the reason this time will be different.

lessons.prompt: What does Samson say about his uncut hair that goes beyond the angel's original announcement?
options: He spells out what cutting it would mean for his strength
He is the first to connect the uncut hair to lifelong dedication
He identifies the Philistines as the people Israel must be saved from
He explains which foods his mother was to avoid while pregnant
lessons.explanation: Judges 13:5 announces the dedication and the uncut hair. In 16:17 Samson makes the consequence of shaving explicit.

teen.picturePrompt: The loom belongs to a failed attempt, and the hair to a secret disclosed later. Which episode brings them together?

bonuses.prompt: Why is the apparently personal question between them not purely private?
options: The Philistine rulers initiated it and offered Delilah silver for the information
Samson asked Delilah to announce every answer publicly
The rulers already knew the secret and wanted Delilah merely to hear it
bonuses.explanation: A conversation that looks like an exchange between two people serves a plan beyond the room.

bonuses.prompt: What change explains why Delilah again calls the rulers after failed trials?
options: This time she sees his hair has already been cut before he speaks
This time she believes Samson has told her his whole heart
This time Samson freely asks her to summon the rulers
bonuses.explanation: The change in her judgment of his words precedes the cutting of his hair.

lessons.prompt: When Delilah questions his love because he keeps a secret, what is she doing?
options: Asking him to give up the reward
Making disclosure a test of love
Warning him to flee from the leaders
Offering to keep his secret from her guests
lessons.explanation: She ties telling the truth to proving his affection, adding to the pressure on him.

lessons.prompt: Why does the reader hear about the Philistine leaders’ offer before hearing Samson confide in Delilah?
options: It proves Samson accepted the same bargain
It tells us that the leaders already know his secret
We can see a danger in his trust before he sees its result
It shows that he and Delilah planned the outcome together
lessons.explanation: Knowing what the leaders want changes how we hear a conversation that Samson treats as personal.

a.picturePrompt: Grain and a grinding stone wait in a room. In which story must the hands that once carried a gate now work inside a prison?

bonuses.prompt: How can we tell this room is for working and for keeping Samson inside?
options: It has two grinding stones
It has grain and a basket
It has a grinding stone and a barred window
bonuses.explanation: The stone is for work. The bars show that Samson is a prisoner.

bonuses.prompt: His hair starts growing. What still stays the same?
options: Samson is still working in prison
All his hair still lies cut on the floor
He is still sitting beside Delilah
bonuses.explanation: His hair has changed, but he has not left prison.

lessons.prompt: Which happened before Samson's hair started to grow again?
options: His family came to take him home
He stood by the two pillars
A boy led him by the hand
His hair was cut
lessons.explanation: In the previous story his hair was cut. In prison it began to grow again.

lessons.prompt: What changed for Samson in Gaza since his visit with the gates?
options: Then he was thirsty; now he was at a spring
Then he left; now he had to stay
Then he walked alone; now he rode a horse
Then he was a baby; now he was a boy
lessons.explanation: He once walked out with the gates. This time he was kept in prison there.

bonuses.prompt: What do we know by the end of the prison episode, and what remains open?
options: His strength has returned, but his hair has not grown
He has already left, but we do not know his destination
His hair has started growing, but we have not yet seen what he can do
bonuses.explanation: The narrator mentions hair growth after the prison work. No new feat of strength has yet been told.

bonuses.prompt: What changes in the use of Samson’s strength between the gate and the grinding stone?
options: At the gate he makes his own choice; in prison others choose his work
In both places he freely works for the people of Gaza
In both places someone orders him to carry a heavy load
bonuses.explanation: The arms that once let him escape are now put to forced labor.

lessons.prompt: The narrator mentions Samson’s hair again. What did his mother learn about it before he was born?
options: It was to be left uncut
It would turn white as soon as he grew up
She had to braid it every morning
It would stay short all his life
lessons.explanation: The messenger told his mother that no razor was to touch her son’s head.

lessons.prompt: Why does hearing the name Gaza again make the prison scene surprising?
options: His parents named him in that city
He found honey at that city's gate
He once left that very city carrying its gates
The angel first met him in that city
lessons.explanation: The same city is the setting for his earlier escape and his present captivity.

b.picturePrompt: Earlier Samson carried away Gaza’s gate. Which later event in the same city do the stone and grain now suggest?

c.picturePrompt: Which reversal in Samson’s fortunes at Gaza do the grinding stone and grain recall?

bonuses.prompt: What does the return to Gaza contribute when the uprooted gate is set beside the place of grinding?
options: The same trade of grinding explains the gate-carrying in both episodes
The narrator explicitly identifies the gate’s lintel with the prison entrance
The same city first stages a freely chosen breach and later a body confined to labor
bonuses.explanation: Returning to the city reverses the function of strength without identifying the two buildings.

bonuses.prompt: How does the brief notice of regrowth work between the annunciation in Judges 13 and the prayer still to come?
options: It recalls the sign of dedication while leaving the question of strength open
It announces complete restoration and renders any further request unnecessary
It removes hair from the narrative before captivity begins
bonuses.explanation: Regrowth echoes the prohibition on the razor near the start. The narrator makes no announcement of restored strength here.

lessons.prompt: Which contrast does the account build by mentioning Gaza both at the gate and after Samson's capture?
options: He first arrives there under guard; later his captors leave him free to work
He first rescues someone from the city; later his family comes there to rescue him
He first reaches Gaza at dawn; later he enters it at the same hour as a captive
He first controls his departure; later others take him there as a prisoner
lessons.explanation: The same city frames Samson's chosen movement in 16:3 and his forced movement in 16:21.

lessons.prompt: At the end of Judges 16:22, what can a reader infer by remembering the birth announcement?
options: The sign has returned, so the narrator confirms that his full strength has returned
A sign of his dedication reappears; its consequences are still open
The sign returns only because he has renewed his vow in prison
The sign returns only after God has answered the prayer for strength
lessons.explanation: The birth story gives the growing hair a history. Verse 22 says nothing yet about a vow, a prayer or a recovery of strength.

teen.picturePrompt: Which reversal in Samson’s journey links the hair cut in the preceding episode with the grinding stone at Gaza?

bonuses.prompt: What tension arises when the account of captivity is immediately followed by the regrowth of hair?
options: Release has been narrated before any regrowth is mentioned
The precise length of his hair explains when captivity ends
His body is changing even as his position as a prisoner continues
bonuses.explanation: Regrowth raises a question about the future inside an account of ongoing imprisonment.

bonuses.prompt: Why does Gaza in particular deepen the contrast between carrying the gate and grinding grain?
options: The same city first sees a freely chosen exit and later his confinement
Samson enters the city in the same role in both episodes
The account identifies the gate and prison as the very same room
bonuses.explanation: The repeated city name connects events that reverse Samson’s freedom of action.

lessons.prompt: Why does the detail about his hair growing again catch the reader’s attention?
options: Its cutting immediately preceded the loss of his strength
His hair has never been mentioned before
Grinding at the mill always makes hair grow
The Philistines have promised him freedom if it grows
lessons.explanation: A small change takes on meaning because we remember what happened when his hair was cut.

lessons.prompt: If the account stopped at the growing hair, which question would remain open?
options: Was he taken to Gaza after his capture?
Was he made to work at a mill?
Will this change affect what Samson can do while captive?
Had his hair been cut before he reached prison?
lessons.explanation: The narrator has already described his capture and work, but has not yet shown what the new growth will mean.

a.picturePrompt: Two pillars stand in a hall. In which story does Samson first find his place and then ask for strength?

bonuses.prompt: Who helped with what in the story?
options: He asked the boy for strength and God for guidance to the pillars
He asked the boy for guidance and God for strength
He asked the boy for both guidance and strength
bonuses.explanation: The boy led him to the pillars. Once there, Samson himself asked God for strength.

bonuses.prompt: Samson asked for help at the spring and at the pillars. How did his needs change?
options: At the spring he asked for strength; at the pillars he was thirsty
Both times he asked to find water
He was thirsty at the spring; at the pillars he asked for strength
bonuses.explanation: At the spring he needed water to drink. In the hall he asked for strength once more.

lessons.prompt: What did Samson ask for in his prayer?
options: For an ark to appear
For God to remember him and give him strength
For honey to fall from the sky
For the gates to grow back
lessons.explanation: Samson asked God to remember him and give him strength. The ending remains sad; hurting people is not something to celebrate.

lessons.prompt: What had Samson also done earlier, when he was very thirsty?
options: Asked God for help
Asked the boy to guide him
Lifted the gates
Told a riddle
lessons.explanation: At the spring and beside the pillars, Samson turned to God when he needed help.

bonuses.prompt: How do the crowd and the boy treat Samson differently in the same hall?
options: The boy wants entertainment; the crowd guides him to the pillars
The crowd wants entertainment; the boy helps him reach the pillars
The crowd and the boy both ask Samson to lead them
bonuses.explanation: The people ask to see their captive. The boy beside him helps him find his way.

bonuses.prompt: Compare the request at the spring with the one in the hall. What stays the same and what changes?
options: Both are addressed to a boy, once for water and once for guidance
At the spring he asks God, but in the hall he asks only the crowd
Both are addressed to God, once out of thirst and once to ask for strength
bonuses.explanation: His need changes. Both times he turns to God for help that he cannot give himself.

lessons.prompt: Which people come for Samson after the crowd’s gathering ends?
options: His brothers and his father’s family
His wedding guests
The people who watched Gaza’s gate
The men who tied the ropes at Lehi
lessons.explanation: His family comes to take him home for burial.

lessons.prompt: At Lehi Samson asked God for water. Beside the pillars he asks for strength. What do the two prayers show?
options: He prayed only when his family was there
He always asked for the same gift
He knew he could not manage everything on his own
He could always leave whenever he chose
lessons.explanation: Each prayer comes when there is something he cannot accomplish by strength alone.

b.picturePrompt: The pillars hold up the hall. Which final episode links what happened to Samson in prison with his request to God?

c.picturePrompt: Which scene closing the cycle places the petitioner between two pillars and returns to the question of where his strength comes from?

bonuses.prompt: How does the final prayer place Samson’s strength in relation to its source compared with the prayer in thirst?
options: Only at Lehi does he depend on an answer; in the hall regrowth alone suffices
Both address God; at the spring he seeks to preserve life, here strength for a final deed
Both prayers ask for a return to life under guard in Gaza
bonuses.explanation: Both prayers express dependence. Their different ends prevent a simple reading of one as a repetition of the other.

bonuses.prompt: What public frame does the narrator set beside the personal desire for vengeance voiced in the prayer?
options: He closes by counting the rulers who paid Delilah before the cutting
He closes with the spring named for the first prayer
After the family burial, he closes by counting Samson’s years as judge
bonuses.explanation: After the final deed and burial, the account records twenty years judging Israel, widening the frame beyond the motive voiced in the prayer.

lessons.prompt: Which two locations link Samson's early stirring by the spirit to his burial?
options: Zorah and Timnah
Etam and Lehi
Gaza and Hebron
Zorah and Eshtaol
lessons.explanation: At the end of Judges 13 and again at the end of Judges 16, the narrator locates him between Zorah and Eshtaol.

lessons.prompt: The angel promised the child would begin to deliver Israel. How does the narrator close Samson's story?
options: He recounts the same blow and closes with a period of peace throughout Israel
He tells of a blow Samson dies delivering, then sums up the years he judged
He counts Samson's years as a judge from the fall of the Philistine temple
He makes Israel's liberation the express object of Samson's last prayer
lessons.explanation: Judges 16 closes with the deaths, the family burial and the length of his judgeship. It does not announce a period of national peace.

teen.picturePrompt: Samson calls for help twice. Which episode do the pillars suggest here, setting it apart from the call at the spring?

bonuses.prompt: What gap opens between the crowd’s intention in bringing Samson out and his intention in addressing the boy?
options: The crowd asks for a prayer; Samson wants to perform for them
The crowd expects entertainment; Samson wants to reach a particular spot
Both the crowd and the boy know in advance what Samson will pray
bonuses.explanation: His appearance before the crowd takes a turn when he asks to feel the pillars.

bonuses.prompt: Which comparison captures both a similarity and a difference between the prayer in thirst and the final prayer?
options: In both he asks to survive danger and return home immediately
In the first he addresses a person and in the last he addresses God
Both depend on an answer; first he seeks life, finally strength for one last deed
bonuses.explanation: His dependence links the prayers, but the ends he seeks differ.

lessons.prompt: Which part of his prayer points to a personal motive alongside the conflict between two peoples?
options: He speaks of the loss of his sight
He recalls the vineyards of Timnah
He mentions his years as judge
He asks for water as he did at Lehi
lessons.explanation: By naming the harm he himself suffered, Samson makes his desire for revenge explicit.

lessons.prompt: At the gathering, the Philistines credit their god with Samson’s capture. How does Samson’s prayer change the viewpoint?
options: Samson joins the crowd in its thanksgiving
The Philistine leaders turn to Samson for help
The same captive they celebrate turns to Israel’s God for strength
The crowd explains what his mother had been promised
lessons.explanation: The crowd and Samson interpret power differently. The narrator lets us hear each side before the story ends.
